lead: An Arduino is a small open-source board built around a microcontroller. You write one program on a PC, send it down a USB cable, and the board runs that program again and again, reading and writing its pins. That is the whole idea: the PC is for writing only, the board does the work alone afterwards. Students use it for the first working version of an IoT device — a light that blinks, a pump that switches, a sensor value pushed to the cloud. This chapter covers the boards, the IDE, and the ecosystem around them.
prereq: You need: the microcontroller-versus-single-board-computer comparison from Unit 2, Sensors, Actuators and Embedded Hardware.

blocks.text: An Arduino board is a microcontroller plus a crystal, a voltage regulator, a USB-to-serial chip and rows of header pins on one printed circuit board. On the Uno the pins are labelled digital 0–13 and analog A0–A5. The Nano adds A6 and A7; the Mega has far more of both. Power pins are 5V, 3.3V, GND and Vin. A digital pin can be an output, where the board drives it to 5 V (HIGH) or 0 V (LOW), or an input, where the board reads whether it is high or low.

Uno, Nano and Mega are 5 V boards. The Uno and Mega have a barrel jack that takes 7–12 V, and an onboard regulator makes the 5 V. The Nano has no barrel jack: power it from USB, or feed 7–12 V into its Vin pin, which goes through its own small regulator. The Nano is an Uno squeezed onto a breadboard-sized board with the same chip; the Mega is wider because it carries more pins and more memory.

Choose by counting pins first. If the project needs four sensors, three relays and a display, add up the pins before buying. Flash holds the program; SRAM holds the variables while it runs. The Uno's 2 KB of SRAM is small — a few long text strings and you are out of room. You cannot add RAM the way you add a stick to a PC. Shrink the code (flash-resident strings, smaller variable types) first, and move to a bigger board only when that is not enough.
The IDE is one program on the PC with three jobs: write, verify, upload.

items: Write the sketch in the editor. The file ends in .ino and holds two functions: setup() runs once at power-on, loop() repeats forever.
Pick the board under Tools → Board, and the serial port under Tools → Port.
Verify (the tick button). This compiles the C++ into machine code for that exact chip and reports syntax errors before any hardware is touched.
Upload (the arrow button). The board resets, a small bootloader already burned into flash listens on the USB serial line for a moment, receives the binary and writes it.
Open the Serial Monitor to watch printed values: Serial.begin(9600) in setup, Serial.println() in loop.

blocks.text: Verify is not upload. Verify only compiles on the PC and nothing reaches the board. Upload fails if the wrong port is picked, or if another program is holding that serial port open.

The board package (Board Manager) adds support for chips the IDE does not ship with, such as ESP32 or ESP8266. Install it once and the board appears in the Tools menu. Names vary between syllabi — some call the program a sketch, some call the language Arduino C/C++. Both are fair: the file is .ino, the language is C++, and the board package supplies the matching C++ compiler — AVR-GCC for the Uno's ATmega328P, another toolchain for other families.

A library is code someone else wrote and tested. Adding one inserts a #include line at the top of the sketch, and a servo, an SD card or a Wi-Fi module then takes about ten lines to drive. The IDE ships with a standard set — Servo, Wire for I²C, SPI, EEPROM — and the Library Manager supplies thousands more.

A shield is a board that plugs straight into the Arduino headers. Motor, Ethernet and GSM shields line up with the pins so no wiring is needed, and the shield's own library knows which pin does what. Shields can stack, but they fight over pins; check which pins each one claims before stacking two.

The design is open, so many companies sell Uno-compatible clones at lower prices. They use the same IDE; a few need a CH340 USB driver installed on the PC first. Some Arduinos — Due, Nano 33, MKR series — run at 3.3 V, so check the logic level before connecting a sensor. The Uno pin layout has become a de-facto standard, and most shields assume it even when the board is different.

figure.caption: One sketch travels from the PC over USB into the Arduino, which drives pin 9 through a 1 kΩ resistor and an LED to ground. The 3 mA loop current is fixed by the 5 V pin, the 2 V LED drop and the 1 kΩ resistor.

spec.title: From sketch to LED
spec.aria: Block diagram shows a sketch uploaded from a PC over USB to an Arduino, which drives an LED through a 1 kΩ resistor to ground.

examples.question: An Arduino Uno runs at 5 V. An LED with forward voltage 2 V is connected from pin 9 to ground through a 1 kΩ resistor. (a) Find the current through the LED. (b) Find the power wasted in the resistor. (c) Write the sketch lines that blink the LED at 500 ms on and 500 ms off, and state the blink frequency.
steps: The pin is at HIGH (5 V) feeding the resistor, the LED and ground at 0 V. So 5 V is shared between resistor and LED.
The LED holds about its forward voltage, V_f = 2 V. The resistor takes the rest: V_R = 5 V − 2 V = 3 V.
Ohm's law gives the current: I = V_R ÷ R = 3 V ÷ 1000 Ω = 0.003 A = 3 mA. Here R = 1000 Ω is the resistance and I is the current in amperes.
The usual working limit of an Arduino pin is about 20 mA, so the pin can source 3 mA directly.
Power in the resistor: P = I² × R = (0.003 A)² × 1000 Ω = 0.009 W = 9 mW, so any quarter-watt resistor is safe.

BLINK. In setup: pinMode(9, OUTPUT); In loop: digitalWrite(9, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(9, LOW); delay(500);. Delays are in milliseconds, so one cycle takes 500 ms + 500 ms = 1000 ms and the frequency is 1 ÷ 1 s = 1 Hz.
examples.answer: The pin current is 3 mA, the resistor dissipates 9 mW, and the sketch blinks the LED at 1 Hz.

traps: A 5 V output wired straight into a 3.3 V sensor input. Check the sensor's absolute maximum first; use a resistor divider or a level shifter.
Forgetting the series resistor. An LED without one pulls far more than the pin limit and both can die; always compute I = (V_s − V_f) ÷ R and keep it well under 20 mA.
Verify is not upload. Verify only compiles on the PC; nothing reaches the board until you upload.

Putting one-time setup code inside loop(). setup() runs once; loop() repeats without end, as fast as its own code allows — thousands of times a second for an empty loop, once a second if it contains delay(1000). So motor or display initialisation must sit in setup().
delay() takes milliseconds as a whole number. delay(500) is half a second, not 500 seconds and not 0.5 ms.

quiz.q: Name the two functions every Arduino sketch must have. How often does each run?
quiz.a: setup() runs once after power-on or reset; loop() runs repeatedly, forever, after setup() finishes.

quiz.q: State the operating voltage of an Arduino Uno, its number of digital pins and its SRAM size.
quiz.a: 5 V logic, 14 digital pins (6 of them usable for PWM), and 2 KB of SRAM.

quiz.q: Why does an ESP32 board need a board package installed in the IDE, while an Uno works straight away?
quiz.a: The IDE ships with core files only for the chips it supports by default, such as the ATmega328P on the Uno. A board package adds the compiler settings, pin definitions and upload tool for a different chip family, after which that board appears in the Tools menu.

quiz.q: What is a shield, and what is one risk of stacking two shields?
quiz.a: A shield is a board that plugs directly into the Arduino headers, with a matching library. Stacked shields can claim the same pins, so one shield's signals may clash with another's.

quiz.q: An LED with forward voltage 2 V is driven from a 5 V pin through a 220 Ω resistor. Find the current. Is it within the usual 20 mA working limit?
quiz.a: V_R = 5 V − 2 V = 3 V. I = 3 V ÷ 220 Ω = 0.0136 A = 13.6 mA. Yes, it is below 20 mA, but with little margin.

quiz.q: A loop holds the LED on for delay(200) and off for delay(800). Find the period, the frequency and the duty cycle.
quiz.a: Period = 200 ms + 800 ms = 1000 ms = 1 s. Frequency = 1 ÷ 1 s = 1 Hz. Duty cycle = 200 ÷ 1000 = 0.2, that is 20 % on-time.

quiz.q: An upload fails with a port error, yet the board is plugged in and the sketch has no syntax errors. Give two likely causes and the fix.
quiz.a: Either the wrong serial port is selected under Tools → Port, or another program (Serial Monitor, a terminal, another IDE) holds that port open. Fix: select the correct port, close whatever is using it, then upload again. A missing USB driver on a clone board causes the same symptom.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the Arduino IDE is often replaced by PlatformIO inside VS Code, or by the command-line tool arduino-cli, because both build and flash from a script and fit into continuous integration. Arduino cores also exist for other chips, so the same sketch style runs on ESP32, STM32 and Renesas boards. Teams move to vendor HALs or to Zephyr when they need a real-time operating system. Search next for PlatformIO, arduino-cli, the Arduino core for ESP32, and Zephyr device drivers.
